title: Present Perfect: Time and Experience
summary: Connect the past with the present, and distinguish unfinished periods from finished past time.

explanation.heading: Experience and relevance now
explanation.body: Use have/has + past participle for experiences when the exact time is not specified, or for past actions with a present result.
explanation.example: Have you ever attended an international conference?

explanation.heading: For and since
explanation.body: Use for to describe a duration and since to identify a starting point. A continuing state often takes the present perfect.
explanation.example: She has worked here since 2021. / They have lived here for four years.

explanation.heading: Finished time
explanation.body: Use the past simple with a finished time reference such as yesterday, last week or in 2018.

exercises.feedback: Since 2021 identifies the start of a situation continuing to the present.

exercises.prompt: Have you ever ___ a technical conference?
exercises.feedback: Ever asks about experience at an unspecified time; attended is the past participle.
Yesterday is a finished past-time expression, so use past simple.
A continuing situation can use has lived or has been living in this context.
Yet commonly appears with a negative present perfect: have not finished.

exercises.prompt: How long ___ you known your colleague?
exercises.feedback: Present perfect questions place have before the subject.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I have sent the report yesterday.
exercises.feedback: Yesterday calls for past simple, not present perfect.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: She works here since 2020.
exercises.feedback: A continuing situation from 2020 to now takes the present perfect or present perfect continuous.
acceptedAnswers: She has been working here since 2020.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: He has gone home last night.
exercises.feedback: Last night is a finished time, so use past simple.

exercises.prompt: I ___ this type of sensor before, so I know what to expect.
exercises.feedback: Before with no finished past-time reference often describes prior experience.
The adverb already commonly appears between has and the past participle.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We have been here since three hours.
acceptedAnswers: We have been here for three hours.
exercises.feedback: For indicates duration; since identifies a starting point.

learningObjectives: Distinguish unfinished time from finished time.
Use for and since with continuing situations.
Ask about life experience without giving a finished time.

left.label: For
left.example: We have tested it for two hours.

right.label: Since
right.example: We have tested it since noon.

examples.sentence: I have never used that interface.
examples.note: An experience at an unspecified time.
Yesterday places the event in finished past time.

examples.sentence: Have you already checked the firmware?
examples.note: Already often highlights completion or surprise.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I have finished the test yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: Use past simple with an explicit finished time.
A continuing state starting in the past normally uses present perfect.

studyTips: Look for time markers: yesterday and last year versus ever, yet, since, and for.
Ask whether the period is still connected to the present.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say that you have already finished the task.
acceptedAnswers: I have already finished the task.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use have + already + past participle for a completed action relevant now.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say that you have not seen the new prototype yet.
acceptedAnswers: I have not seen the new prototype yet.
I haven't seen the new prototype yet.
speakingExercises.feedback: Yet commonly appears in negative present perfect sentences.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask a colleague whether they have ever used Python.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use Have you ever + past participle to ask about experience.
